subject: wizardBookshelf
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: wizard's bookshelf with tomes, scrolls, orbs and candles.
Style: high-fantasy anime.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for a wizard's bookshelf prop, deciding to include a root joint even though it's a simple prop, and mapping out which builder methods I'll need like part, extrude, lathe, and sweep to construct it safely.

Now I'm sketching the full design: a dark wood bookshelf with an arched crown, carved trim, gold accents, five shelves, side posts, and a star-textured navy back panel, topped with a crescent moon ornament. I'm figuring out contents too -- colorful merged books, scrolls, glowing orbs on lathe pedestals, candle holders with wax drips, and maybe a potion bottle or hourglass, while keeping part counts manageable. I'm settling on overall dimensions of roughly 1.5m wide, 0.42m deep, 2.3m tall, with a small plinth base and bun feet.

Working out shelf heights and compartment spacing, I'm defining five shelf levels plus a taller top compartment for candles and orbs, topped by an arched pediment crown bringing total height to about 2.65m. Now I'm starting the helper function for constructing boxes with width, height, depth, and color parameters.

I'm planning the material and paint strategy: wood grain textures applied via paint rather than counting against the color budget, with sides using a vertical grain axis and shelves using a horizontal one. For the book palette, I'm sketching out roughly ten cover colors plus gold trim, with each book built from a colored cover box and a cream page block.

Now I'm setting up a batching strategy to merge geometries by color at the end, reducing part count by collecting translated/rotated geometries per color and merging them via BufferGeometryUtils before adding a single part per color group.

I'm sketching the book structure for the shelf: each book is a box with thickness, height, and depth, spine facing outward, with separate colored cover and page geometries to keep the look realistic while staying within triangle budgets.

Settling on a real multi-part book structure: a front spine board, two side cover boards, and an inset pages box that peeks slightly above the covers, plus a gold band and label on the spine. That's four boxes per book plus bands, so 80 books ends up around 4k triangles total.

For tilted books, I'm building each one in local coordinates with the origin at the bottom center, then rotating about the z-axis and nudging it upward slightly so the tilted corner doesn't clip through the shelf. For lying/stacked books, I'm generalizing the same book function to accept a yaw rotation so it can be laid flat with thickness, height, and depth reassigned along different axes.

I'm simplifying by centering each book's geometry at its own local origin, then composing a transform of translation times yaw rotation times tilt rotation to place it. For standing books I need to position the center at the shelf height plus half the height, accounting for any lift from the tilt angle at the base corners.

I work out the general formula for vertical offset: the half-extent after tilting combines cosine of height and sine of thickness, which correctly reduces to just half the thickness when a book lies flat. I accept that leaning books at row ends may slightly overlap neighbors, since it's visually negligible, and now I'm sketching the shelf's inner dimensions, accounting for the side panel thicknesses to get the usable interior width.

Now I'm figuring out depth placement: given the shelf's inner z-range and back panel thickness, I calculate where book centers and spines should sit so they don't poke through the back panel, adjusting book depth and front alignment so spines sit naturally near the shelf front without excessive recession.

Then I'm moving on to the overall frame structure—sizing the plinth board and planning small corner feet (octagonal cylinders) that support it, deciding their height and placement relative to the plinth's vertical range.

Next I'm defining the sides of the frame as tall boards flanking the plinth, figuring out their width and vertical span so they align with the shelf boards' total width, and adding a front moulding detail along the plinth's top edge for decoration.

Then I'm placing the shelf boards between the sides with proper depth, laying out a top cornice board with overhang, and stacking a stepped moulding piece above it before shaping a pointed arch pediment using an extruded outline along the width.

I'm also building a crescent moon shape for the pediment center by computing outer and inner arc points geometrically, plus a lathe-style finial with a star on top.

I work out the intersection points at (0.625, ±0.78), giving an angle of about 51.3° on the outer circle, and translate those into the inner circle's local angles of roughly ±77.4°. Now I need to figure out which inner arc segment—the one carving the concave crescent edge—connects these two points without crossing outside the outer boundary.

I want the crescent opening to face up-right rather than sideways, so I'll rotate the outline points by about 30-35 degrees to get that "☾" look. I also need star outlines using sharp-cornered five-pointed shapes, and then I'm setting up the pediment extrusion mounted on the front face of the cornice.

Working out the depth placement now: pediment at z=0.1 with thickness 0.06, decorations like the moon and stars layered just in front of that, and considering adding a slightly larger gold border extrude behind the main shape for a trim effect.

That rim stays visible but slightly recessed from the front, which works fine. For the back panel, I'm considering adding a star-field texture with a navy-purple gradient and sparkles, placed to face forward where it'll peek through gaps above the books; painting the pediment face with scattered star dots directly seems more promising than trying to fit a rectangular plane into the arch shape.

Writing cell-based star paint...

Given the uncertainty around which helpers are actually exported, I'm weighing lower-risk options: maybe use svg for the back panel geometry since that's clearly documented, and rely on cells/gradient only for the pediment stars and wood grain texture, minimizing dependence on functions I'm not fully sure are exported.

For the back panel, I'm designing an SVG viewBox sized to match the panel's aspect ratio, with a navy-to-purple gradient, scattered star sparkles, a faint teal arcane circle, and constellation lines, making sure stroke widths stay thick enough to survive rasterization at the chosen texture resolution.

I'm adding the textured back plane as a part positioned behind the box, using a white base color so the texture renders correctly, and now I'm double-checking whether SVG-based textures actually load properly in this sandbox environment.

I'm also planning the shelf contents layout — dividers separating compartments, with the top shelf holding a row of large tomes on the left and a scroll rack with a cubby on the right.

For that scroll cubby, I'm figuring out how to render stacked scrolls end-on as circles facing the viewer, with a darker center disc suggesting the rolled spiral, plus a tiny hole and ribbon detail for realism, arranged in a pyramid within the cubby space.

Adding darker end caps, center holes, and thin ribbon cylinders for color variety, with around 14 scrolls merged by material. For the shelf above, I'm planning leaning books from x=-0.67 to 0.15 plus a glowing orb on a pedestal stand at the right side.

I'm sketching the orb pedestal as a lathed brass base, stem, and claw cup holding a sphere with a bright core color, considering a layered card with radial gradient alpha to fake a soft glow halo since true emissive materials aren't available.

Instead of a halo card, I'm deciding to texture the orb sphere with a swirling nebula pattern in cyan/violet plus white sparkle decals and tiny octahedra floating around it for extra sparkle detail.

I'm using a radial gradient centered on the rect for the sphere's light-to-dark shading, with smooth sphere geometry at modest segment counts. For shelf two, I'm planning tall tomes and a flat book stack with a candle, plus deciding to add a simple lathed hourglass with sand and wooden end caps instead of a skull for visual interest.

Building the hourglass geometry...

I'll color the upper bulb pale blue glass and the lower bulb gold sand for a convincing look without real transparency. For shelf 3, I'm planning books on the left and a candle cluster on the right—varying candle heights on a brass plate with flame cones.

For shelf 4, I'm laying out a magenta orb on a stand, a tall candle atop a stack of tomes, and possibly a rolled map and small violet potion bottle elsewhere, checking that stand heights stay within the 0.30 compartment clearance.

Now I'm thinking about the top of the cabinet itself—whether a full pediment spanning the whole width would block any decorative items placed there, or whether a narrower central peak design would leave room on the cornice ledge for a crystal ball or owl figure in front of it.

I'm placing decorative pieces on the cornice ledge: an amber orb on a pedestal at the left, a stack of books with a candle on top at the right, with the pediment curving between them. I'm also adding lathe-turned finials at the four corners of the cornice for extra ornamentation.

Now I'm designing the front corner columns -- thin eight-sided cylinders with gold base and capital rings, and wrapping a tight gold spiral wire around each column using a sweep-along-spiral helper to simulate twisted trim.

I'll go with 5 sides for the sweep, placing corner columns slightly protruding beyond the side panels so the cornice and plinth overhang properly. For the color palette, I'm planning a dark walnut wood grain for painted sides, shelves, top, plinth, pediment, and columns, with gold accents for trim.

Actually I want a more vivid anime high-fantasy feel: a rich deep plum-brown wood with gold trim, a navy starfield interior back panel, and vivid book colors—crimson, royal blue, teal, emerald, violet, amber, rose, ivory, orange. I'm tallying part counts (sides, shelves, columns, merged book colors) to stay well under limits, and double-checking the flat color budget stays within 64 while listing out specific hex values for each book cover color.

Continuing to tally colors for scroll ribbons, wax and candles, flame layers, and orb/potion details like glass, sand, and cork tones.

For the candles themselves, I'm working out geometry for wax cylinders, wax drips, wicks, and layered teardrop-shaped flames, plus a generalized placement helper that handles position, rotation, and scale. Now I'm sketching the brass candle holder with a lathed dish and a torus ring handle.

For the lathe-based parts I'm planning cross-section outlines for orb stands, candle dishes, finials, and a potion bottle, defining each as a profile of points rotated around an axis to form the solid shape, starting with the orb stand's cup profile.

Checking the polygon closes cleanly along the axis without crossing itself. I'm working out the sphere placement: with cup radius 0.05 and orb radius 0.09, the center sits about 0.17 above the base so the sphere's bottom nests into the cup around y=0.08. I also want to add four prong-like claws gripping the orb.

Rather than fiddling with tilted cone claws, I'll go simpler with gold armillary rings — two tilted toruses wrapping the orb at different angles for a wizard-staff look, plus tiny octahedron sparkles scattered around in white and cyan for a magical touch.

I'm planning the orb placements per shelf with distinct colors and sizes, and sketching helper functions for generating orbs and candles (with drip variation and optional dish). I'm also considering small floor props like a stack of books near the shelf, though keeping the overall composition centered and within bounds.

Settling on a left floor stack of tomes with a melting candle for balance, and on the right a small cluster of potion bottles made from merged sphere and cylinder shapes to vary their silhouettes.

For randomness, I'm deciding whether to rely on the SDK's rng(seed) function or roll my own deterministic generator — since the spec says randomness must flow only through a passed-in rng, I should stick with the SDK's version even though its exact return shape isn't fully clear to me.

Since I'm unsure if rng returns a plain function or an object with methods, I'm writing a small wrapper that checks its shape and normalizes it to a callable random function, trading a bit of elegance for safety. Now I'm moving on to the book row generator, which walks across a shelf width placing books with randomized thickness and height within given ranges.

For the final book in a row, I want it occasionally tilted toward the shelf gap, which means leaving extra space and applying a positive rotation so its top leans toward negative x, matching a leaning stack of books.

Now I'm working out book decoration: gold bands at fixed height fractions on the spine, occasional cream label plates on every third book, and bigger tomes getting a clasp or gold diamond accents on the cover.

Then I'm figuring out the local geometry for each book -- spine board, side covers, and the inset page block -- positioning each piece relative to the book's thickness, height, and depth so the pages sit snugly between the covers with cream-colored edges peeking out.

I'm also placing the gold decorative bands on the spine face, offsetting them slightly from the surface so they protrude naturally, before starting on the title label.

For flat-lying stacks, I need to check how rotating by 90 degrees reorients the spine so it faces up correctly, and confirm the gold bands end up running across the spine as vertical stripes rather than horizontal ones.

I'm setting up the transform pipeline: build each book's geometry locally, then apply a composed matrix that translates into position and rotates by yaw then tilt, so normals and lighting stay correct. For the generic put() helper, I'm defining it to take a color, geometry, position, Euler rotation, and scale, building local box geometry and translating it before the final transform is applied.

Then I group geometries by color in a batch map so I can merge them per-color at the end for efficient rendering. But I realize merging will break for the octahedron shapes, since PolyhedronGeometry is non-indexed while boxes, cylinders, spheres, and toruses are indexed -- mergeGeometries can't mix those, so I need to handle that mismatch separately.

I'll add a single root joint to be safe since props can be plain objects without joints, and set up a box-building helper function along with wood paint textures using grain patterns for different parts.

For color palette, I'm leaning toward a deep aubergine-brown wood tone to fit an anime fantasy feel — settling on grain colors like "#5b3345"/"#3d2030" for vertical pieces and a slightly warmer tone for horizontal shelf surfaces.

Now I'm sketching the pediment gradient in navy-purple with gold trim, plus star extrusions and a moon shape. I'm also working out shelf positioning constants — side panel location, shelf heights spaced along the vertical axis, and board thickness for the physical layout.

Working out plinth and trim dimensions...

Checking the back panel depth and confirming books won't clip through it, then placing front corner columns spanning the full shelf height with gold base and capital rings for the base/capital detail.

I'm now working out the gold spiral winding around each column using a helix with fixed radius and pitch, calculating turns needed to cover the column's full height.

Then I'm shaping the triangular pediment outline point by point, trying to get an ogee-like curve that starts shallow near the base and steepens into a pointed peak near the apex.

I'll close the shape going counterclockwise back to the base, keeping the apex and base corners sharp while skipping heavy smoothing to avoid self-intersection errors, and apply a small bevel instead. For the gold border, I'm computing a scaled-up outline offset slightly to create the rim effect.

Now I'm positioning the pediment element with its origin and orientation, setting the thickness so the border and face sit at the right depth, then placing the star and moon elements just in front of that face at the correct z-offsets.

I'm adding a small teal gem (octahedron) beneath the moon as a finial accent, and considering whether to sketch gold ribs along the pediment's top edge before deciding to skip that detail. I'm also checking how the item positions align with the cornice's front ledge height.

Now I'm placing an orb on a stand near the pediment's edge, accepting the slight overlap since it sits in front, and planning four small lathed finials at the corners -- doing both front and back even though the back ones stay hidden. Writing finial outline coordinates...

I'm double-checking the finials' positions won't collide with the pediment's edges or cornice depth, confirming the radius and z-range keep them clear in front of and behind the structure.

Now I'm setting up the inner compartment coordinates and a color palette array for book covers, then writing a helper function that generates rows of books with randomized thickness, height, depth, and color.

I also need to handle the leaning book at the end of each row — reserving a bit of space so the last book can tilt against the shelf edge with its corner anchored near the row's end.

I'm second-guessing the geometry of the leaning book: really the top should rest against the neighbor while the bottom sits offset by roughly h*sin(angle), meaning the book leans toward the row rather than away from it, with its lower corner pulled back from the support point.

With that, I'm deriving the horizontal shift from center to bottom-center using half the height times sine of the tilt plus half the thickness times cosine, so I can compute the center x/y directly for either leaning direction. I'm reserving extra horizontal space in the row for the lean (about h*sin(a) + t ≈ 0.11) so the tilted book doesn't collide with the row boundary.

Confirmed the rotation direction works for the lean effect. Now I'm laying out the first shelf's compartments, placing a row of tall tomes with a reserved lean slot, then adding a vertical wood divider panel to split the compartment.

I'm working out a pyramid arrangement of scrolls in the cubby area, calculating radii and vertical spacing row by row, but find the full five-row stack exceeds the shelf height so I cap it at four rows totaling fourteen scrolls.

Now I'm detailing the scroll geometry itself: varying lengths and z-offsets so some stick out at different depths, adding darker end caps with a central hole, and a colored ribbon band wrapped around the middle with a tiny gold seal to suggest a tied scroll viewed from the end.

I'm also adding a standing scroll case near the divider — a thin violet leather tube with gold bands, positioned to fill the gap between the lying scrolls and the divider for visual variety.

For the first shelf, I'm placing a row of leaning books followed by a decorative orb on a lathe-turned stand, checking that the combined height stays under the shelf's upper bound, and considering a small stack or candle to fill the remaining space beside it.

For the second shelf, I'm working out room for a tall book row on one side and an hourglass near the center, adjusting positions so the leaning books and hourglass widths don't overlap.

For the center, I'm settling on a 2-book stack topped with a candle on a dish, checking that the flame still clears the shelf above by a safe margin, with a second row of books on the right needing a minimum height around 0.25.

Now I'm sizing up shelf three's available height and planning shorter books on the left side within a max height of 0.30.

For shelf three's right side, I'm placing a brass plate with three varied candles and drips, plus a cluster of potion bottles and maybe a rolled map.

Then for shelf four, I'm positioning a magenta orb on a stand at the left, a row of tall books in the center, and on the right a stack of flat tomes topped with a small candle and star decoration, carefully checking the candle height so the flame just clears the shelf above.

Now I'm working on the cabinet top and floor arrangement: an amber orb on one side balanced by a book stack with candle on the other, then floor-level clusters -- a leaning stack of flat books topped with a wax-dripped candle on the left, and a trio of varied potion bottles with spheres, necks, and corks on the right, all checked against the model's bounding limits near the floor and sides.

Checking overall height, I realize the pediment apex would push the cabinet too tall at over 3 meters, so I'm scaling the pediment outline down (roughly to 0.56 of its original size) to keep the apex around 2.8m total while still looking appropriately wizard-like, and sizing the moon ornament to fit proportionally within the narrower pediment width at that height.

Working out positions for the moon, stars, and gem within the scaled pediment outline so they fit inside its tapering width without overlapping the edges.

Confirms the star placements fit within the outline bounds. Now I'm building the back SVG with a gradient-filled sky background...

Adding stars, sparkles, and arcane circle details...

Adding swirl paths and sparkle highlights...

Now I'm sketching a candle helper function that builds the wax body as a tapered cylinder, with optional wax drips rendered as thin capsule shapes placed around the rim.

Shaping the flame as a teardrop sphere with a cone tip, then sizing the candle wax radius and building the dish as a lathe shape with a simple outlined profile that closes cleanly around the axis.

Deciding to swap the dish's lathe geometry for a cheaper merged cylinder approach instead, saving lathe for orb stands, finials, and similar small decorative pieces. For the hourglass, I'm assembling it from merged parts: top and bottom discs, corner posts, and glass bulbs for the upper and lower sand chambers.

I'm sketching out a merged potion bottle function too: a flattened sphere body, neck cylinder, lip ring, cork, and a label band, plus a small highlight sphere for shine.

Tallying up the color palette across books, scrolls, wax, candles, flames, hourglass, and potions, I'm landing around 48 distinct colors with reuse elsewhere, comfortably under the 64 limit.

Writing the orb function...
